decisions.quote: We successfully replicate the prior Nie et al cross-validation results using a newer version of their data that is publicly available.
decisions.reason: The direct re-test of Nie et al. (2018)'s TRD cross-validation finding re-analyzes the same underlying STAR*D clinical trial dataset (using the public NIMH Data Archive release and partial code/hyperparameters from the original authors). Under the codebook, re-analyzing the original study's own data is a reproduction regardless of the authors' use of the word 'replicate'; the separate CAN-BIND-1 analysis is an external validation of models trained on STAR*D predicting 8-week QIDS-SR response/remission rather than TRD.

decisions.quote: Nie Z, Vairavan S, Narayan VA, Ye J, Li QS. Predictive modeling of treatment resistant depression using data from STAR*D and an independent clinical study. PLOS ONE. 2018;13: e0197268.  pmid:29879133
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify the same original study, Nie et al. (2018), PLOS ONE 13: e0197268 (DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0197268). The blind coder left the DOI blank only because the reference list prints the article number e0197268 without the full DOI string.

decisions.quote: The highest balanced accuracy was higher in our study compared to Nie et al (73% versus 71%, respectively). Similarly, our highest AUC was higher at 0.81 versus 0.78, respectively. The z-score of Nie et al’s results in our distributions ranges from -0.4 to -34.
decisions.reason: Because the record type is reproduction, outcome must be coded on the two reproduction axes. For outcome_computation, re-implementing the STAR*D pipeline produced comparable metrics but did not recover the exact original numbers (2520 vs 2454 subjects, 480 vs ~700 features, 70%-73% vs 64%-71% balanced accuracy, z-scores from -0.4 to -34), which corresponds to 'computational issues'. For outcome_robustness, across the alternative holdout split, reconstructed feature sets, and alternative target/scale specifications tested on the STAR*D dataset, the substantive predictive finding remained supported and the authors judged the differences clinically insignificant ('robust'). Parent checked the corresponding Discussion interpretation: Regardless, our slightly improved performance is unlikely to be clinically significant, and we instead interpret our results as a successful replication supporting the findings of Nie et al. and our own implementation of data processing and machine learning methods.
